Introduction/Concepts

Concepts

Use these concepts to make AI-assisted development easier to direct and review. Each section explains a practical problem, a way to address it and a small example.

An AI agent is software that uses an AI model and tools to carry out a task. The concepts below explain how to define that task, support the agent and review its work.

These are related practices rather than lifecycle stages. The recommendations and examples are guidance for discussion and do not represent EDS policy.

On this page

How the concepts fit together

The concepts address different parts of the same work. Intent-driven development explains why a change is needed. Spec-driven development defines what the software should do and how the team will check it.

Context engineering supplies the information an AI agent needs. Harness engineering provides its tools, permissions and checks. Loop engineering defines how it responds to feedback; graph engineering organises steps and dependencies. A software factory brings these practices into a delivery workflow.

For example, a team wants users to resume an unfinished service request. The team agrees the goal, writes acceptance criteria, gives the agent the relevant information and tools, and reviews the result. Model selection supports that work.

The service-request examples throughout this page are fictional. Read the sections relevant to your task; the concepts are not steps that every change has to follow.

Intent-driven development

Intent-driven development means agreeing why a change is needed before choosing a solution. Record the user’s problem, the intended outcome and the limits the solution needs to respect.

Use it when a request leaves room for conflicting interpretations. “Improve the form” could mean a new layout, fewer questions or a way to save unfinished work. Agree the user need before asking an agent to implement a solution.

Agree the outcome and constraints

  • Problem: who is affected, and what prevents them from completing their task?
  • Outcome: what should the user be able to do after the change?
  • Constraints: which access rules, data-handling requirements or existing behaviours need to remain?
  • Open questions: what is undecided, who will resolve it and when is the decision needed?

Example · Help users resume an unfinished request

Users leave a long request form to find supporting information. When they return, their entries are gone. The goal is to let them resume the request without re-entering the same information.

Saving a draft should not submit the request or notify a reviewer. Only the request’s owner can reopen it. The product owner will use user feedback to decide whether an explicit “Save draft” action is enough or automatic saving is needed.

Keep the record proportionate

A short issue may be enough for a small defect. A new capability may need research and a product requirements document. Recording a goal does not establish that it is valuable; test important assumptions before committing substantial effort.

Next step: Write the problem, outcome and constraints for one change. Then use the product thesis guidance to test the case for it, or define its acceptance criteria when the need is understood.

Source: [1].

Spec-driven development

Specification-driven development, or spec-driven development, uses written requirements to guide development and review. The specification describes the expected behaviour, including important exceptions and constraints. Acceptance criteria state how the team will judge whether that behaviour works.

Use it when a broad request leaves developers or agents to guess the details. “Saving works” does not explain what happens when a connection fails, another user requests the draft or two browser tabs make changes.

Use the requirements to guide both development and testing

Before development, the specification informs the technical design and tasks. During review, tests and reviewers compare the working software with the same acceptance criteria. Keep design choices in the technical plan so developers can choose how to meet the requirements.

Example · Describe what “Save draft” means

The team chooses an explicit “Save draft” action. It agrees these acceptance criteria before implementation:

  • Incomplete form: saving keeps the entered values without submitting the request.
  • Successful save: show “Draft saved” after the server confirms it. Reopening the draft restores the saved values.
  • Failed save: retain the values on screen, explain the failure and offer a retry.
  • Access control: reject another user’s attempt to read or change the draft, including requests made outside the browser interface.
  • Conflicting edits: if another browser tab has saved a newer version, explain the conflict and preserve the unsaved values.

Add detail as decisions become clearer

Too little detail forces the team to invent product rules. Too much detail before research can make an untested idea look settled. Resolve important unknowns, then update the specification as the team learns. Human review still covers judgements that automated tests cannot settle.

Next step: Check one requirement for its success, failure and access-control cases. Use the requirements handover checklist, then translate it into technical design and development tasks.

Source: [2].

Context engineering

Context engineering means selecting and maintaining the information an AI agent needs for its current task. That information can include requirements, relevant code, team standards, test results and earlier decisions.

Use it when an agent follows an outdated rule, misses a business meaning or cannot find a decision. Supplying more documents alone does not solve the problem. Give the agent the relevant information and a clear way to find further detail.

Choose relevant, current and authoritative sources

Start with the task’s goal, acceptance criteria and constraints. Add the code and standards needed for the change. Confirm the applicable source with its owner when documents disagree. Record important decisions where the next person or agent can find them.

Example · Add an “Awaiting review” filter

An agent is asked to add an “Awaiting review” filter to a list of service requests. The label does not tell it which records belong in that state.

Provide the agreed status definition, current access rules, the relevant code and an existing filter test. Mark an older document’s “Pending” label as superseded. The developer then checks that the browser displays the right records and retains the filter when the page is reopened.

Keep decisions available beyond the conversation

Save decisions, unresolved questions and progress in the repository or issue tracker. A future session needs access to those records to use them. Keep source versions where they affect the decision, and follow the applicable data-handling rules.

Relevant information improves the basis for the work; it does not guarantee a correct result. Review retrieved material before relying on it. A document or log does not gain authority merely because an agent found it.

Next step: List the information missing from one recent task. Use the context-by-stage guide to identify the right source, then prepare and check that source.

Source: [3].

Harness engineering

Harness engineering means designing the tools, permissions, checks and progress records around an AI agent. This supporting environment is the agent’s harness. It lets the agent do the work, observe the result and stay within agreed limits.

Use it when an agent cannot run the application, check a result or resume unfinished work. A better prompt cannot replace a missing test environment or an access control.

Provide the tools and controls the task needs

The six components below are one way to describe the supporting environment. They work together rather than running as six consecutive steps.

  • Agent state: what the agent is doing now and what it will try next.
  • Tools: the actions it can perform, such as reading files, using a browser or running tests.
  • Memory: saved decisions, progress and reference information that later work can retrieve.
  • Orchestration: how tasks are assigned, ordered and handed over.
  • Safety: permissions, allowed actions and limits on time, attempts or spending.
  • Observability: records of actions and results that help people investigate and review the work.

Example · Test a file upload

An agent adds attachments to a request form. Its harness provides the running application, a test account, sample files and test storage. The agent uploads a file, checks that it was saved and opens the saved attachment.

The test account cannot reach production storage. If test storage is unavailable, the agent records the blockage and stops. Seeing an upload button is not proof that uploading works.

Check the environment as well as the output

Provide a repeatable way to start the application, run tests and inspect failures. Enforce permissions through the tools and execution environment. Keep a reviewer responsible for acceptance; an agent’s assessment of its own work is not independent review.

When failures recur, inspect the instructions, sources, tools and checks before adding more retries or access. Maintain the harness as the application changes.

Next step: Check whether a developer can start the application, run its tests and inspect a failure using the documented setup. Follow the Eitri installation guide and team setup checklist to fill the gaps.

Sources: [4]; [5]; [6].

Loop engineering

Loop engineering means designing how an agent uses feedback to improve its work over several attempts. A feedback loop connects an action, an observed result and a decision to continue, change approach or stop.

Use it when a task needs repeated correction, such as fixing a failing test. Define the expected result before the run starts. Also agree how long the agent may try and when it needs help.

Define the check and every way to stop

A loop can start when a person requests it, an event occurs or a schedule runs. Each attempt needs a check of the actual result. Save progress between runs so later work can continue from the record.

Example · Fix search results that arrive out of order

A user types “printer”, then “printer paper”. The first search response arrives last and replaces the newer results. The developer creates a browser test that reproduces that order.

The agent changes the code and reruns the test. It returns passing results for review, or stops after three unsuccessful attempts. If the test environment is unavailable, it records the blockage instead. The three-attempt limit is illustrative.

Keep the success criteria unchanged during correction

A loop can repeat a bad assumption as well as correct a defect. Check that the tests represent the intended behaviour. Do not weaken a test merely to finish the run; review a requirements change separately.

Keep a record of what the agent tried and what each check found. Another agent may offer useful review, but can share the same mistaken assumptions.

Next step: For one repetitive task, write down the success check, run limit and person to contact when blocked. See how the developer workflow builds, tests and corrects a change.

Source: [7].

Graph engineering

Graph engineering, as used here, means designing a workflow of tasks and dependencies. The graph shows what can run next, what needs to wait and where a person makes a decision. It can include feedback loops.

Use it when several activities need coordination. Some tasks can run together; others depend on a prior decision or another task’s output. A workflow graph makes those relationships visible. It can describe one agent or several.

“Graph engineering” is an emerging label. Here it refers to workflow design, rather than a knowledge graph of facts and relationships.

Agree the dependencies before splitting the work

In the example, the browser and server teams first agree an application programming interface (API) contract: the data exchanged and expected behaviour. They can then work separately and test the combined result.

Example · Build “Save draft” across the browser and server

The team agrees which draft fields to save, who may access them and what happens when two tabs make conflicting changes. One developer builds the browser states; another builds storage and access checks on the server.

Both return their changes and test results. The team then checks the real browser against the real server. If the server work is incomplete, the combined test waits. If the combined test fails, the relevant developer corrects the issue before a fresh check.

Add coordination only where it helps

More tasks and agents mean more handovers, cost and opportunities for conflicting changes. Give each task clear inputs, outputs and ownership. Record which tasks completed and how a stopped workflow can resume without repeating an external action.

A box labelled “approval” does not enforce approval. Configure the tools and workflow to respect the required decision, and keep release permissions within the agreed authority.

Next step: Mark the dependencies between two related tasks. Identify what they can do in parallel and the check they need together. Use the story-planning guidance and the task review and approval steps.

Sources: [8]; [9].

Software factories

In this guide, a software factory brings requirements, agent work, testing, review and release controls into a repeatable delivery workflow. The aim is to turn agreed work into changes that the team can check, release and support.

Use the idea when individual coding tasks are fast but work still waits for clarification, review or release. Improving one task does not remove the constraints elsewhere in delivery.

Choose how people review and approve changes

Addy Osmani uses “light” and “dark” factory to distinguish review arrangements. In a light factory, a person reads changes before release. In a dark factory, permitted changes can be released without that reading step. These are operating choices, not levels of maturity.

For an unattended route, agree which changes are permitted, what checks are needed, who can pause it and how to recover. Running a coding task without supervision does not itself authorise merge or release.

Example · Handle a queue of service-request fixes

The team receives a reproducible search bug, an unclear upload error and a request to let managers read every draft. The first two can become development tasks. The access change waits for a product and permissions decision.

Agents work on the agreed fixes in isolated environments. Tests and a preview help a reviewer inspect the result. Approved changes follow the team’s release process; new defects and feedback return to the work queue.

Keep understanding and recovery alongside automation

Track review waiting time, rework, defects and cost before increasing throughput. Keep design decisions available and practise diagnosis and recovery. A passing test suite does not show that people can explain or repair every change.

A preview is not a production release. Preserve the approval, monitoring and recovery controls needed for the action being taken.

Next step: Choose a small group of changes and measure where they wait. Use the automation and approval guidance, then review the release checks.

Sources: [10]; [11].

AI models

An AI model is trained on data to recognise patterns and produce outputs. Depending on the model, those outputs can include text, analysis or a choice from defined options. Model selection means choosing and testing a model for a particular task.

A convincing answer to one question does not show how a model will handle other tasks. Compare models on realistic examples, including difficult cases and missing information.

Understand the labels before comparing options

The labels below describe different properties and can overlap. A small model can specialise in a domain; a large model can do so too.

Model labels and what they mean
TermMeaningExample task
Large language model (LLM)MeaningA language model with many parameters: numerical values learned during training. Used for tasks such as drafting text and explaining code.Example taskDraft acceptance criteria or explain code.
Domain-specific language modelMeaningA model trained or adapted for a subject area’s language and tasks.Example taskWork with specialist service terminology.
Small language model (SLM)MeaningA language model with fewer parameters than larger alternatives. Consider it when computing resources or local operation matter.Example taskClassify a service request.
System One, from TypeSafeMeaningTypeSafe’s name for models such as Jev that answer defined questions with choices or probabilities.Example taskSelect a request category from agreed options.

A defined output format or a confidence score does not establish that an answer is correct. The model examples and research below explain the distinctions and limits.

Example · Compare models for a service-request task

Give each candidate model the same request examples, category definitions and supporting information. Keep a separate set of examples for the final comparison so decisions are not judged only on cases used to adjust the setup.

Record incorrect categories, response time, running cost and cases that need human review. A model that drafts helpful text may not be the best choice for classification; compare each against the task it will perform.

Model examples and research
Four dimensions of model choice
DimensionLabelsWhat to assess
ScaleLabelsLarge or small language modelWhat to assessCapability, memory and compute needs
SpecialisationLabelsGeneral-purpose or domain-specificWhat to assessPerformance on the domain’s language and tasks
Output interfaceLabelsGenerated text or typed decisionsWhat to assessWhether the task needs writing, a choice, a score or a probability
Reasoning approachLabelsFocused judgement or deliberative reasoningWhat to assessWhether the task needs one bounded judgement or extended analysis

Large language models (LLMs)

LLMs learn from extensive datasets and can support varied tasks through instructions and examples. Modern model families combine language generation with capabilities such as reasoning, image understanding and tool calling. OpenAI’s GPT-5 documentation describes coding, reasoning and agentic tasks with configurable reasoning effort; GPT-5.4 provides a newer example with text and image inputs, structured outputs and tools for multi-step work. [12] [17]

Anthropic’s Claude Opus family provides another example. Opus 4.5 supports extended thinking, while the later Opus 4.8 supports adaptive thinking. Both accept text and images and return text. These capabilities become useful in a development workflow when the harness supplies relevant context, tools and checks. [18] [19]

Read the references in two ways: model documentation explains supported inputs, tools, reasoning controls and limits; model or system cards describe the provider’s evaluations and limitations. Compare candidates on your own tasks with the same context, tools and acceptance criteria. Check the provider’s current catalogue and lifecycle guidance before choosing a version. [20]

Use and limits: consider a general-purpose LLM for varied drafting, explanation and coding work. Larger size alone does not establish quality on your task. Compare correctness, latency and cost using representative examples, including cases where evidence is missing.

Domain-specific language models

A domain-specific language model is trained or adapted for the terminology and tasks of a field, such as finance or biomedicine. Specialisation can use domain-focused training, continued pretraining or task fine-tuning. Gururangan and colleagues found benefits from continued domain and task pretraining across their classification experiments. [13]

BloombergGPT illustrates that specialisation and scale can coexist: its 50 billion parameters were trained using financial and general-purpose data. Its reported gains concern the evaluated financial tasks, not every specialist application. [14]

Use and limits: consider specialisation when domain language causes recurring errors and suitable training data exists. Compare it with a general model supplied with relevant reference material. Retrieval supplies context at use time; it does not by itself retrain the model. Here, “domain-specific” refers to a subject area, not a domain-specific programming language (DSL).

Small language models (SLMs)

SLMs use fewer parameters than larger alternatives, usually reducing model storage and memory needs. There is no single parameter threshold used consistently across model families. The Phi-3 report describes Phi-3-mini, a 3.8-billion-parameter model small enough for phone deployment, trained with carefully selected and synthetic data. [15]

Use and limits: consider an SLM for bounded tasks such as request classification or field extraction, especially when local operation matters. Measure performance on the intended hardware. Small size does not guarantee fast responses, accurate answers or private operation; deployment and data handling still matter.

System One model (System 1)

“System 1” is an analogy for fast, intuitive judgement, contrasted with slower, deliberate “System 2” reasoning. TypeSafe AI uses System One for a model class that turns application state and predefined questions into typed decisions and probabilities. Its model, Jev, supplies focused judgements that application code can combine into a workflow. This product meaning is more specific than asking an LLM to answer quickly. [22] [23]

What Jev receives and returns: its documented input is text, including strings, JSON objects and arrays of text. It evaluates questions against that state and returns constrained answers rather than writing a reply or code. The three question types are: [23] [24]

  • Choice: select from defined options, such as the team that should receive a ticket; return the choice and a probability distribution.
  • Score: assess the state against defined, ordered levels, such as an urgency rubric; return a score and probabilities across those levels.
  • Noul: estimate the probability that a statement is true, from 0 to 1, such as whether a request mentions an outage.

Questions in the same request are evaluated independently against the same state. Code combines their answers, checks permissions and decides the next action. If a later question needs an earlier answer, build a follow-up request with that result. Open-ended writing and complex reasoning can remain with a generative model or a person. [24]

Confidence needs interpretation: Choice and Score include a confidence statistic derived from their probability distributions. Noul returns a yes/no probability without a separate confidence field. Confidence is not proof of correctness, and a valid output type does not establish that the judgement is right. Check accuracy and calibration on representative, held-out cases before setting thresholds for action, further analysis or human review. [25]

What the evidence supports: TypeSafe reports speed and cost gains on its own workflows; those gains depend on the comparison and deployment conditions. A separate 2026 preprint, Fast Models, Slow Evidence, found Jev stronger than the compared model on many decision points, but both performed at chance on its zero-shot model-routing task. It also showed how omitted costs and thresholds fitted on evaluation data could overstate deployment benefits. This is early, task-specific evidence rather than a general guarantee. [22] [26]

Example · Triage a service request with Jev

Supply a request’s text, relevant service details and the triage rubric. Ask separately for its category, urgency and whether it reports an outage. Application code applies the validated routing rules. Uncertain, conflicting or uncovered cases go to a person; an LLM can draft a response when needed. Keep access and release approvals in their existing decision process.

Related research: Yu and colleagues’ System 2 distillation work concerns training models to answer directly from reasoning-derived examples. GPT-5 reasoning effort and Claude thinking controls vary deliberation within generative models. These are related ways to balance computation and quality, but they do not establish the typed-decision interface that defines Jev. [16] [21] [18] [19]

Evaluate the complete task

Use the information, tools and permissions that the model will actually receive. Compare results with the current approach, including rules or human handling where relevant. A smaller model does not guarantee speed or privacy, and a larger one does not guarantee better results.

Next step: Choose one task and agree its acceptance criteria before comparing models. Use the testing and independent review guidance, and retain cases where a model fails for future checks.

Sources and learning references

The references support the explanations on this page. The examples illustrate the practices; they do not establish organisational requirements.

Learning references

Use these courses, guides and playbooks for detailed instruction and practice. Check the implementation courses for prerequisites and tool requirements.

  • Intent-driven development: CircleCI’s guide explains how to carry outcomes, constraints and success criteria through a change.
  • Spec-driven development: AI Agent Factory crash course covers specifications, planning and implementation tasks.
  • Context engineering: Context engineering resource collection gathers techniques, research and a learning roadmap. Read the intent-driven.dev overview for the concept’s role in defining requirements.
  • Harness engineering: Walking Labs provides explanations, projects and templates. The AI Agent Factory crash course adds practice with controls and verification.
  • Loop engineering: Iwo Szapar’s playbook provides a design canvas. The AI Agent Factory crash course covers triggers, saved progress and checks.
  • Graph engineering: AI Agent Factory crash course develops parallel branches, checking and merging.
  • Software factory: Vercel Academy provides an implementation course. Addy Osmani’s article discusses review arrangements and the limits of autonomy.
  • Models: start with GPT-5 and GPT-5.4, or Claude Opus 4.5 and Opus 4.8, for examples of reasoning and tool-supported work. Read the GPT-5 prompting guide for reasoning controls and the matching Claude model card for provider evaluations. Use domain adaptation research, BloombergGPT, the Phi-3 report and System 2 distillation research for the underlying concepts.
  • System One and Jev: read TypeSafe’s System One explanation, question primitives and confidence guidance, then compare its provider claims with the separate evaluation preprint. Start with one bounded decision and measure it against your current approach.

  24. TypeSafe, Primitives (Questions). Defines Choice, Score and Noul, independent questions and composing answers in code.

  26. Li (2026), Fast Models, Slow Evidence: A Paired and Self-Audited Evaluation of System-1 Decision Models for LLM Agent Harnesses. Preprint comparing Jev and Laya; reports decision-point results and limitations in routing, threshold selection and deployment accounting.

The model examples illustrate capabilities and trade-offs. Provider documentation covers product behaviour; the research papers explain underlying concepts. Evaluate the exact version and configuration you will use.
